utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour. Good afternoon, everyone in the court. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Today is Monday, the 5th of November, 2007. I would like to greet the Prosecution, the Defence, as well as the accused. After a few days of interruption, we resume the proceedings in this case. The Trial Chamber will now deliver a number of decisions, and I will read them out slowly. Decision regarding to the admission of P 09781. In a decision dated 14th of February, 2007, under Rule 92 bis the Trial Chamber decided not to rule -- or to stay its ruling regarding the statement of the 4th of July, 1994, of Becirovic, expecting the production by the Prosecution of an English translation, of a proper English translation of the statement. The statement dated 4th of July, 1994, is marked P 09781. It is annexed to the 92 bis statement of Dzevad Becirovic. That statement was admitted by a decision taken on the 14th of February, 2007. In a motion filed on the 4th of October, 2007, the Prosecution submitted a new translation, a new English translation of Exhibit P 09781. In so doing, the Prosecution stated that this translation, the translation thus submitted, was the integral or complete translation in English of P 09781, whereas the first translation that had been submitted was a summary in English of the B/C/S version of the document. The Prosecution explained that this summary was submitted with its previous motion because only the summary had been certified by the presiding officer as part of the proceedings provided for by Rule 92 bis. The Trial Chamber notes that the Defence has not responded to the motion filed by the Prosecution. The Trial Chamber has decided to admit Exhibit P 09781 because it shows indicia of reliability, probative value, and credibility. The Trial Chamber states that only the complete translation in English of Exhibit P 09781 should be -- should be found in the e-court system, and therefore we invite the Prosecution to make sure that this document is uploaded into the system instead of the summary of the B/C/S version of the document. For obvious reasons related to the probative value of the evidence, the Trial Chamber invites the Prosecution only to submit full translations of the exhibits it seeks to tender. The Trial Chamber will now hand down a new decision related to the extension of time for -- to respond to six motions filed by the Prosecution. On the 30th of October, 2007, the Defence requested an extension of time of two weeks to respond to six motions filed by the Prosecution. On the 1st of November, 2007, the Prosecution responded. The Chamber's legal officer told you about it last week. She announced that the Trial Chamber had decided to grant the request partially and to give two additional weeks except for two motions, and I'm now going to deal with these two particular motions. The first motion relates to -- is the motion by the Prosecution requesting the admission of Exhibit P 09848. This motion was filed on the 25th of October, 2007. The Trial Chamber has decided that the Defence should respond by tonight, by midnight at the latest. Second motion, it's the motion filed by the Prosecution requesting an addition to the 65 ter list, addition of Exhibit P 10327. This motion was filed by the Prosecution on the 26th of October, 2007. The Trial Chamber requests the Defence to respond at the latest tonight at midnight. A further decision related to the motion filed by the Petkovic Defence in order to be granted enough time for the following witness. On the 30th of October, 2007, the Petkovic Defence requested five hours in order to cross-examine the witness, Witness Pringle. The Prosecution, on 1st of November, opposed that request. Following the reading of the expert report submitted by the witness, the Trial Chamber believes that it will be sufficient to grant one hour to the Petkovic Defence, one hour to the Praljak Defence, and 30 minutes to the Defence of the other four accused. As a result, the application made by the Petkovic Defence is dismissed. Let me add that the other Defence teams are free to offer their time to the Petkovic Defence if they believe that the Petkovic Defence team would be in a position to conduct the entire cross-examination of the Witness Pringle on its own. Let us now go into private session. Let me add that each of the other four accused will have 30 minutes each. Private session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Further oral ruling related to the application made by the Prosecution to upload in the e-court system Exhibit P 00626. On the 8th of October, 2007 the Prosecution asked to be authorised into the e-court system Exhibit P 00626. The Trial Chamber has decided to grant this request. However, we would like to ask the parties -- we would like to ask both the Defence and the Prosecution to check in the future, together with the Chamber's legal officer and the representative of the Registry, therefore to make the necessary checks before submitting such motions. Technical checks should be made beforehand in order to avoid any mistakes. Let me also tell the Defence that a few minutes ago the Trial Chamber filed a decision related to the -- the application made by the Prosecution to admit a number of testimonies under Rule 92 bis. This is related to Stolac and Capljina. This decision is about 30 pages long, and it was filed and registered with the Registry. Before I give the floor to Ms. Alaburic, I would like to ask the registrar to go back into private session for a few minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours. We're in open session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With regard to the oral decision rendered today, according to which the Defence will be allocated a certain amount of time, the Petkovic Defence is aware that there is no legal remedy with regard to the decision taken today, and we submit a request to file a complaint in relation to that decision. I'd like to remind the Chamber, I assume that they are informed of the fact, I'd like to remind you that General Petkovic's Defence, as soon as they were informed about the time allocated to the various Defence teams, filed an application to file the complaint on the 1st of December [as interpreted], and we stated in a number of pages that the rights of our client had been violated, the right he should have if he were to be tried on his own. His right to appropriate time for cross-examination has been violated, so has his right to a fair trial has been violated. We will submit a written version of the complaint. I don't want to spend any more time on presenting my arguments, thank you very much --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: And the date was on the 1st of November, interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I was going to mention that as well, Your Honour, but can I just say that I don't think that the translation here or the interpretation does complete justice to Ms. Alaburic. It was just, to make it clear, it was an application for certification to appeal against the rejection of our application to have more time for cross-examination of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [No interpretation] Let's introduce the witness now.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Several parties have submitted lists of documents to be tendered through Witness Ray Lane. The list submitted by OTP shall be given Exhibit number IC 700. The list submitted by 2D shall be given Exhibit number IC 701. The list submitted by 3D shall be given Exhibit number IC 702. The list submitted by 4D shall be given Exhibit number IC 703. One of the parties have submitted lists of objections to document tendered by the OTP through Witness Ray Lane. The list submitted by 5D shall be given Exhibit number IC 704. The OTP has also submitted a response to exhibits tendered by accused Praljak for witness Ray Lane. The list submitted by OTP shall be given Exhibit number IC 705. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. The registrar will now introduce the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Hello. I hope that -- that you understand what I'm saying translated into your language. You were asked to come here by the Prosecutor's office to testify for the needs of the transcript please give us your name, surname and date of birth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Andrew Pringle, 9th of October, 1946.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is your professional present current occupation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm a retired military officer, currently a consultant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You were retired military man. What level, what grade, what rank.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I retired as a major general.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, have you ever testified before this court before or is this the very first time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have testified before this court on two other occasions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you remember which cases you testified before?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The first case was the Dubrovnik case and the second case was the Vukovar case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very good. I would like you to read out the solemn oath.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, General. You can sit down now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, there's some very quick data. This is the third time you have come before this Tribunal. You are aware of the procedure. In the first place you will be answering questions raised by the Prosecution, and I think you met with a member of the OTP on the basis of a report that you drafted and on the basis of various documents that are given to us in two files that you have before you, normally. And after that series of questions the Defence, which is on your left, there are many lawyers there, generally there's only one lawyer for one accused, and sometimes the accused themselves take the floor because of the highly technical nature of the matter we are dealing with, so they will be asking you questions in the framework of the cross-examination. The four Judges that you have before you, they are not military personnel, but they do have some knowledge of these affairs. They, too, will at any point in time be asking you questions, but they would in fact prefer that the parties involved have priority except for documents that require immediate elucidation. We will be having breaks every hour and a half so that you can rest, and this will also give us an opportunity to change the tapes. If at any point in time you do not feel well please make it known to us, and I will interrupt for that purpose. And if you wish to ask the Judges any questions, please do not hesitate to do so. So those are, in general terms, the way that we shall proceed. We have three days ahead of us, Monday, Tuesday, and Wednesday, three hearings, except that tomorrow we will be having our hearing, unless I'm mistaken, in the morning, whereas on Wednesday -- well, actually, on Wednesday in the morning, too -- or, rather, the afternoon. I'm not quite sure. I think it's the afternoon. So in any case, tomorrow morning we shall be having the hearing at 9.00 and you will be come back here, and Tuesday at 14.15. We have three days in all. Mr. Scott, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Good afternoon, General Pringle. Are you reasonably comfortable there? I don't know if your chair needs to be --

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: No, I'm comfortable but I don't have any files here.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: We'll get those to you shortly. We might not need them for a few minutes perhaps, but in any event, they will be brought to you at the appropriate moment. General, I would like to discuss briefly this afternoon a little bit about your background. Unfortunately, given the time that's available to all of us we cannot cover your considerable CV and accomplishments in detail, although that has been provided in full to all the parties and the Judges. So they will have the benefit of a much longer treatment, if you will, of your curriculum vitae than we will have a chance to cover in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I do state for purposes of the record, Mr. President, that his CV is essentially in the report which has been marked as Exhibit P 09549.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Having said that, sir, if I could just lead you through a few of the perhaps more pertinent aspects of your background for purposes of your testimony here, and you have been called as a Prosecution expert witness for the purposes of talking about command and control concepts in a somewhat in an international setting. So for that reason I'm going to focus on a few features of your background to touch upon command and control and on your international experience.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To save time perhaps, Your Honour, some of the time that we spent earlier on, on behalf of General Praljak's Defence, I would like to say that in this portion of the curriculum vitae and the professional qualities of the witness, we won't mind if the Prosecutor uses leading questions to save time, and I'm sure the other Defence counsel will agree with me but of course that stops after the introduction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine, yes. We have the CV of the witness, so please go to the essential points you want to highlight for us.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I think the Chamber may know from my past practice that on these background matters I do generally tend to ask leading questions for these purposes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So, General, if you'll allow me and I'll just ask you what you've just heard described as leading questions, if you could just confirm some of the more pertinent aspects of your experience, please. Of course we know that you're a retired major general from the British Army. You retired in 2001 after 37 years of active service; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your first operational tour of duty was in -- was part of a United Nations force in Cyprus; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: What was the approximate time period of that deployment?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: That was 19 -- it was for six months in 1967, I think it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Following that, you did a number of tours of operation or duty, if you will, in Northern Ireland, I think 1971, 1972, 1973, 1978, 1979, 1980, and 1981, 1983; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You also had a command position for a time in Berlin, and I understand that during that time you exercised regularly with the French and American units of the Allied Powers Berlin; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Then I understand that you also spent time commanding the Royal Green Jackets, a unit for the British Army, again in Germany and in the UK, and in these circumstances you also had close contact with the German army and was exposed to German army doctrine and operating procedures.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You also completed a one year course at the Royal College of Defence Studies, and my understanding is that this course was made up half of members of the British military primarily, perhaps some other police and other governmental positions always well. The other half of the course was drawn from around the world, predominantly from persons in military positions. The course content was set at the strategic level and involved considerable study about the political military interface in the defence environment; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And the courses speakers and daily interaction provided a greater understanding of common military issues, common military doctrine, and ways of operating; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Moving to another command position in Germany in 1994, you then served for a time with the US peacekeeping force or Implementation Force in 1995 being the commander of UN Sector South west based in Gornji Vakuf; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: It was with the UN force, not the US force, and I was the UN commander Sector South-west.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I misspoke, my apology. The UN force. And at that tour lasted approximately how long?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: Six months.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Is it correct, sir, that you then returned for a second tour in Bosnia and Herzegovina during the period 1997, 1998?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: What was your position or function at that time?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: I was the commander of multinational division south-west based in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And in the course of your military experience, sir, is it correct that you have commanded troops not only from the United Kingdom but in fact troops from Spain, Turkey, the Netherlands, Canada, the United States, the Czech Republic, New Zealand, and Malaysia?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Is it also correct that you have cooperated closely with headquarters and troops from Australia, France, Germany, Sweden, Norway, and Finland during the course of your career?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: During the course of your military career, sir, and in particular as part of your courses at the Army Staff College, you received particular training in military law and the international laws of war, or armed conflict?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Is it correct to say that as part of your military career you have taught and lectured on a number of occasions to senior military officers on command and control?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: That's correct, and I've also carried out a number of studies on command and control for NATO.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And, sir, what I've tried to highlight this afternoon very briefly in your curriculum vitae is that in addition to your time in the British Army, is it fair to stay you have been exposed to a number of international settings and the military doctrine of a number of armed forces?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: Yes, I think that's fair.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And finally, sir, just to bring us up to the current time, I think you mentioned briefly, you are now doing some sort of consulting work?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And is that related to defence industry?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: That's defence industry related and a lot of contact current contact with the Ministry of Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And just finally again in your -- it's in your CV but is it correct for the Judges to understand that you have essentially commanded troops yourself at all, essentially all unit levels from the level of a platoon up to the level of at least a division?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: I have commanded at every level from platoon to division, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now, moving beyond your military background just to touch on a couple of other matters. The president has already asked you but I'll just confirm again that you previously gave testimony in the Strugar case concerning Dubrovnik; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And you also gave testimony, expert testimony, in the Mrksic case which you described a few moments ago as the Vukovar case; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, in your report itself,?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And I think perhaps now is as good a time as any if we could provide the witness, please, with the two binders of documents.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You may not need to refer to your report now, but I am referring to what is set out in paragraph 2, just to talk about the taskings that you were given by the Office of the Prosecutor, the scope of the work you performed, and is it correct that you were asked to look at essentially three principal questions, one being to explain the nature of command and control in military organisations by drawing on personal experience; number two, comment on the normal military-political interface, in general between senior military commanders, civilian Defence Ministers and commanders in chief; and three, offer professional opinions on the military significance of a number of documents provided by the Prosecution? Is that a fair summary of your taskings?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Before moving on, sir, in this same regard it may be helpful to point out, ask you what was not within the scope of your report, and the Judges will not see in your report but nonetheless just to make clear. General Pringle, there maybe some who would see that one potential role of a military expert witness would be someone who would look -- study particular facts, look at maps on a board, look at perhaps figures representing armies on a board and explain past campaigns, past battles, military history in that sense. Now, you've not been asked to do that; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: I have not been asked to do that in this case and have not been provided any material to do that with either.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And as part of the work you've done for the Office of the Prosecutor in this case, have you looked at any specific operations or battles, if you were -- if you would, within the context of the conflict between the HVO and the ABiH in the time period 1992, 1994?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: I have examined a number of documents that were given me, but all more in the context of command and control and the three subjects you raised earlier rather than in any context of detailed battles or the conduct of those battles.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. And I take it from your CV and some of the facts that we covered just a few moments ago that while you did have two tours of duty in Bosnia-Herzegovina, you were not in theatre so to speak between 1992 and early 1994?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: That's correct. That's -- well, I visited -- I was not in operational command between 1992 and 1994, although whilst I was serving in the cabinet office I did pay a visit to Sarajevo in 1992, I think. More as a fact-finding mission rather than anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, with that in mind and turning specifically then to the content of your report, can you confirm to the Judges that the content, the observations, the conclusions that you state in your report are your conclusions and yours alone? There's not been any particular direction or -- in that respect given to you by the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: That's correct. Everything I have written in this report is -- is -- are my own thoughts, reflections, and my own work.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, if you can turn - I think you perhaps already have - to a copy of your report that's in the binder which again is Exhibit P 09549. Just looking at that for a moment, and I'm sure you've seen it in the last few days, is that a true and accurate copy of the report that you prepared in connection with your work for the Office of the Prosecutor in this case?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And on the face of the report I see that it was originally signed by you, I believe, on the 26th of March 2006; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can the Judges correctly understand that since finishing your report at that time in March 2006 that you have had occasion perhaps from time to time and again more recently to look at that report?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: I have refamiliarised myself with this report recently, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And do you continue to stand by the observations made and the conclusions stated in report?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If we had more time, General, and if I were to take you through your report essentially in a line-by-line fashion, can the Judges understand that what is written in your report would essentially be the testimony that you would give in the courtroom?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Sir, now with that background in mind I would like then to turn to some particular questions about your report, recognising again that all the other participants in the courtroom, the Defence and the Judges themselves, of course, will be able to ask you any other questions about your report if I don't. If I can -- I'm going to march through it pretty much in the order of the paragraphs. With a few exceptions we might jump around but I can ask you and direct the courtroom's attention to paragraph 16. In the first section of your report you talk about the concept of doctrine, and in paragraph 17 you say, and what I'll do in some instances, I'll just read you some part of your report and ask you if you can clarify or comment further, you say: "Put most simply, doctrine is what is taught. NATO describes doctrine as 'fundamental principles by which the military forces guide their actions in support of objectives. It is authoritative but requires judgement in application.' Doctrine has its foundation in history and derives its authority from being the distillation of much hard-won experience. Doctrine is enduring but it is not unchanging. Doctrine is not dogma." Now, when you say, for example, when you say that doctrine was -- or the definition that's given here or your words or somebody else's, when you say doctrine is "a distillation of much hard-won experience," what does that mean?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: That means doctrine drives future conduct, learning from the lessons of the past and -- and forming mindsets, tactics, equipment requirements and everything that follows on from that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In connection with doctrine, then, did you spend a substantial amount of the work that you did in preparing your report looking at the doctrine of the Yugoslav People's Army or what would be called the JNA?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: Yes. I referred to quite a large number of such documents which I have in some instances referenced in this report, and all of which I would describe as doctrine.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And perhaps you can just briefly describe why in this context you particularly looked at JNA doctrine.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: Well, JNA doctrine is readily available. I had think it was formulated in and around 1988. It was the basis of the Yugoslav army's doctrine, and therefore anybody that had been educated, whatever their ethnicity, in the Yugoslav army would have been brought up on that doctrine.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Is it correct, sir, that not all, certainly, but perhaps a substantial majority of the officer corps that joined either of the three armies, and when I say three armies, whether they be Croatian, Serbian or Muslim, that large number - excuse me - of officer corps came out of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour. Your Honour, could we have a foundation for that? How can the gentleman answer that without a foundation? What did he do to make -- to be able to answer this factual question?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right, Your Honour, if it's really necessary, if this is really a disputed point. I'm quite surprised, but if it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, let me talk about your times, your two tours in Bosnia, for example, other courses that you've been involved in. Did you have any reason to understand the history of military doctrine in the former Yugoslavia? When I say history, I mean recent history, in the past 20 years or so?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: Can you formulate that question again?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sure. You've heard the objections of Defence counsel and I'm just asking you if you can explain to us what familiarity you have with JNA doctrine and what relationship, if any, it has to the armies that evolved out of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: I met a large number of officers from all ethnicities during my two tours in Bosnia who had started life in the JNA and who were then serving as either in the Bosnian Serb, Bosnian Croat, or the Armija. They had been brought up as JNA officers. They'd been educated in JNA schools. And whilst I cannot put numbers to your previous question, it's quite plain to me that the foundations of those ex-regular officers of the JNA who now found themselves in one of the three armies had been brought up to JNA doctrine and principles.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And in looking at military doctrine as we're discussing it this afternoon in reference to the former Yugoslavia, can you identify to the Judges any other foundation or basis for military doctrine that would be more logical for us to look at other than -- rather than the JNA?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: No, I can't, and I think I've stated in my report that given the rapidity with which this war broke out, and in particular the Bosnian Croat and Bosnian Muslim factions, simply would not have had time to formulate comprehensive doctrine of their own although -- although from a study of the documents that process was beginning, I concluded as an assumption that their actions would be based on the original JNA doctrine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Your Honours, just a technical question. The witness said that this doctrine was brought in in 1968 -- 1998 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpret's correction: '88. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] So what was the difference between only two generations of officers could have been trained on the basis of that newer doctrine if that was indeed when it was introduced?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So this question goes even further into your answer. Can you answer that? When you talk about the military doctrine, is it timeless or did you see variations depending on the dates? Did they vary from one time to the other? This is a cross-examination question normally, should be, but perhaps to save time we could -- so in your opinion was that doctrine timeless or did you feel that there was slight variations with time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I think I said that the number of documents I think had the date 1983. Perhaps it could have been 1988, but it was around about that period. And let me quote one particularly, the very good doctrine, a JNA doctrine on the application of the international laws of armed conflict. That is timeless, and that -- the doctrine that would have been evolved by the JNA around about that time would, I assume, have been still extant when the war in the former Yugoslavia broke out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There are several generals here, and there's another one that has just raised his hand. General Petkovic. THE ACCUSED PETKOVIC: [Interpretation] Your Honours, thank you for giving me the floor. I'd like to ask the question the following way: A doctrine is a written document, so the doctrine of every country is a written document. Now, if the witness worked on the doctrine that he mentioned, could he tell us more about the doctrine of 1988? So there's no doctrine passed on by word of mouth. A doctrine is a written document; that's the first point. And secondly I think the witness is mixing up doctrine with rules and regulations, so a doctrine is a view of the state not a textbook. When you study doctrine, then you study doctrine on the basis of practice and all the rest of it. So I'd like to refer the witness to the 1988 doctrine where a written document must exist to show that that doctrine was in existence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My learned friend has reminded me that this should be part of cross-examination since now the OTP is doing first examination. Of course the general is hopefully acquainted with this type of subject, and we run the risk here of losing time. General, General Petkovic is making a distinction between doctrine and rules. The rules are something that is -- are enshrined in a written document. Now, are you mixing the two up, or in your view does military doctrine -- is it, too, enshrined in a document? Is -- can we superimpose doctrine and rules?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. In my earlier statement, in my report, I said put simply doctrine is what is taught. Now, doctrine can be enshrined in documents. It will then be taught in military schools. It will be verbalised. It will become taught practice. Regulations or rules might well be or almost certainly are part of doctrine, trying to achieve the same aim. And if I refer once again to the regulations on the application of international laws of war and the armed forces of the SFRY, introduction, very first sentence, "The objective of this book is to acquaint the members of the armed forces of Yugoslavia with the rights and duties of combatants in armed conflict." That is exactly the same as a doctrinal publication on that subject.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I might, Your Honour, and I think to further demonstrate the wisdom of letting the direct examination proceed and saving these kinds of questions and observations and arguments, for that matter, for a later time, the next two exhibits are exactly the written documents, including the 1988 document. So we could have done this ten minutes ago had there not been the improper interventions.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I can ask you, sir, to look at Exhibit 0 -- P 0007.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me interrupt you Mr. Scott. You're quite right, but your answer confuses the issue a little bit. General, if I refer to Mao Zedong's writings in the area of military usage, one can consider that for the Chinese army, Mao Zedong had the biased doctrine, and Mao Zedong, well, his opinion was embodied in rules and regulations. Now, concerning the JNA, is there a military thinker, generals, that devised military doctrine for the JNA and that this was thereafter reflected in regulations or the doctrine as you would have it, is that more the fruit of experience of generations of military men previously and the legislative power inherits, as it were, rules such as the JNA rules. Could you clarify that? When you talk about military doctrine, I'm wondering whether in your mind these are rules or whether you are referring to thinkers in this area, and that -- if that is the case, that could take us very far indeed. Could you perhaps very quickly answer my question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Doctrine is formulated usually in a department of the General Staff of whatever army or navy or air force we're talking about to describe a - drawing on experience and previous practices - to describe the conduct of operations currently and into the fairly near future but not the far future. And it is on those writings that everything that follows in terms of the training and conduct of operations and equipment procurement for the armed services is -- is derived.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: General, if you could then turn, please, to Exhibit P 00007. Four 0s, 7. Which I believe will be the 1988 document that there has been reference to in the past 10 or 15 minutes. And can you tell us -- can you look at Exhibit 7 and tell us what that is, please.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: This is a document that was drawn up by the JNA in 1988 to describe the impact of the international laws of war on the conduct of operations by the armed forces of the SFRY. It draws heavily, obviously, on those international laws of war and associated conventions, including the Geneva Convention, and turns it into a very, in my view, cogent and well-written description of how the armed forces should conduct themselves if they are to be in compliance with those laws to which the SFRY had signed up.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, we're going to look at that document in various more detailed respects in the course of your direct examination. But before we do that, just to round out the documentary foundation, if you will, of this, could you please look at Exhibit 5, P 00005. And when you have that, General, can you tell the Judges, just confirm for the record what that document is.

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: This is the command and control doctrine issued in Belgrade on behalf of the JNA in 1983. So this is laying down best practice on all aspects of command and control.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Would it be fair to say, General, and I think we're coming up on the first break but perhaps I can finish just on these two documents, did both of these documents serve as two of the important foundational documents for the work that you did in this case?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: Yes, they did, and both of these documents, despite their difference in title, would be what I am referring to as doctrine.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Petkovic, I told you that the questions should come up during the cross-examination. If you raise your hand that means there's a major issue. What is this major issue? THE ACCUSED PETKOVIC: [Interpretation] Your Honours, yes, there's a big problem. The task of the expert was different. Expert -- the expert is using document 00005. It's not even doctrine. It's for cadets in military academies. It is commanders of batteries, et cetera. So high officers can't deal with such textbooks for cadets. Military academies for company commanders. And I regret that the expert didn't go to the academy in the former Yugoslavia. He's talking about a textbook that is studied in academies. The JNA has more important documents than this one.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: This is-- this is ridiculous.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, the question that you've raised is a question for the cross-examination. So we take note of that. It's been taken note of, but Mr. Scott must go on. But in any case he will be continuing after the break because we must stop for 20 minutes, and we shall resume in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Alaburic, you wanted to address the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I don't want you to think that I really said what you can see in the transcript, page 23, because there are a few sentences that are quite incorrect. I want to correct this. So on page 23, line 13, I didn't say that there was no legal remedy against the decision on the time for cross-examination. I said that there wasn't an effective means of legal remedy, because the decision taken today is applicable on the day it is rendered. Secondly, I did not say that the request -- that the application for certification to appeal was filed on the 1st of December. I said it was filed on the 1st of November of this year. And thirdly, I did not mention a complaint, a legal remedy as a complaint. I mentioned a legal remedy that is called application for certification to appeal. So this clarifies what I wanted to say. Thank you very much. I an I apologise for this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: General, I don't want to get too bogged down in this issue about doctrine and regulations, but just before we move on, if you look back at -- if you have still in front of you Exhibit 5. On the cover page. At the bottom of the cover page, if I'm not mistaken it has this language: "To be used in teaching the subject the basics of command and control at military academies of the Yugoslav People's Army." Now, I take it is it correct, General Pringle, that doctrine is indeed taught at all the major military academies? I suspect that if we went to the military academy in the UK, Sandhurst, or if we went to West Point in the United States or perhaps if we went to Saint-Cyr in France, you would, one of the things they teach their up-and coming officer corps is military doctrine; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: That's correct. And the doctrine taught is applicable to all levels. To suggest what is taught at a military academy is not appropriate to a senior officer is absurd, in my view.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, just moving on and in paragraph 21, in reference to that, on this point before moving forward is it fair to say that in conducting your work you found that JNA doctrine was the most relevant and most readily available material for purposes of looking at the evolving or present doctrine of the armies or military forces coming out of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And if I can direct your attention in particular to paragraph 22, you gave us some examples, I believe, where you said that some of the terminology, in fact, is closely paralleled between the, for example, the JNA doctrine -- the JNA document that is marked as Exhibit P 000005 with an HVO document which is marked, and we'll look at in a few minutes, P 08128, that the types of functions, for example, the terminology was in fact almost the same. Is that fair to say?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. It -- it appeared to me that the evolving HVO doctrine was very closely derived from the existing JNA doctrine.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In -- just continuing on, in paragraph 23, for example, you say that the HVO doctrine that's stated in Exhibit P 08128 lists the principles of command -- the basic principles of command and control as centralisation, resilience, cohesion, continuity, flexibility, being operational, and security. And again did you find that to be closely parallel to what you found in the JNA documents?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And in fact, sir, even more broadly than the JNA would those elements be common to most military doctrines at that basic level?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: Yes. Those -- those notions are readily recognisable.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So you'd recognise those principles or notions, if you will, for the British Army as well?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: Exactly. Exactly, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In that respect if we could in fact turn to Exhibit -- in the second of the binders, the smaller of the two binders, I believe, but to Exhibit P 08128. And there is a cover of communication to a document that's titled on page 3 of the exhibit, Section I, Command and Control. And if you look at page four of that document, in fact, do you see the words listed under "Principles," the words that I just referred you to a few minutes ago?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And looking down that same page towards the bottom of that page, for example "Norms," we have another list what has been described here or at least what has been translated: "Norms: One man command, subordination, cohesion," et cetera. Once again, is all that terminology consistent with what you saw in the JNA documentation?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And if I can move forward to paragraph 24, just for clarification purposes. You say in that paragraph: "The overall military commander exercises the authority vested in him for the direction, coordination, and control of military forces." When you used the term "overall military commander" in this context, what position -- what position are we talking about? I'm not necessarily talking about which human being but what position in the system are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: Well, really I'm talking there about the military commander at any level from junior to the top-most senior commander. He's -- each one of them is exercising authority based on his legal and constitutional position.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me ask you to turn, please, in the -- I believe we'll have to go back to the first binder to Exhibit P 00289. You reference this document which is, for the record, "the decree on the armed forces of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna." And you refer to this, among other places perhaps, in paragraph 25 of your report. You say in reference to paragraph 25, first of all of you include in statement coming from the document itself. It says: "The defence system of the HZ HB shall be a uniform form of organisation of the armed forces administrative bodies and legal entities. In effect this enshrines political control over the military as one would expect." When you say enshrines military control as one would expect, what do you mean?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: Well, hang on. I say, "enshrines political control over the military as one would expect," that is to say, it certainly is the norm in Western militaries that the military is subservient to the political. So that's what I would expect to see.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Moving on to paragraph 27, you say that "Command refers to the authority vested in an individual for the direction, coordination, and control of military forces. It therefore encompasses the authority, responsibility, and duty to act." Now, my question is you refer to the authority -- not only the authority to act but the "responsibility and duty to act." What -- could you tell us a bit more what you mean by the responsibility and duty to act as separate or something different than the authority to act?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: Yes. The authority to act is the authority again from the legal provisions, but in terms of exercising command and a commander's responsibility, therefore, for the direction, coordination, and control of military forces, he not only has the legal authority but the duty or responsibility to execute it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So is it correct to say it's not enough simply to have the authority to act but there are instances in military -- in the military where you absolutely have the responsibility and duty to actually carry out that authority in other words?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: Absolutely correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You also mention in that paragraph 27, you say that: "Command also involves accountability." What do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: I mean by that every commander is accountable not only for his own actions but for the actions of his subordinates. That's part of the duties of command.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In paragraph 29 you refer to an exhibit -- a document which has been marked as Exhibit P 00095, and you have that, sir, if I can first direct your attention to the first paragraph of the document. It says: "Members of armed forces are required to carry out the orders of superior officers pertaining to service, except for those orders whose execution would constitute a criminal act." Can you comment on that and whether that would be consistent with your experience with most modern armies at this time, including, for example, the British Army?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: Yes. That is a fundamental statement to which all military would be familiar, that is say that being part of the military carries with it the duty to carry out orders, except for those orders which constitute a criminal act as written here. That codifies the notion of an illegal order. If a soldier is given an illegal order, he is -- he is not required, indeed he is absolutely not required to carry it out.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Nozica.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, thank you. I apologise for interrupting, but I believe this is the time for the Prosecution to provide us with information. Perhaps we received this document, but the document doesn't have a date. There is no signature on it. The expert has used it, but to know which period it relates to, to know the date of the document, we ought to know the source. We should at least approximately know what the date is. All that we have as a date in the document is a reference on the first page to disciplinary and material responsibility. It says: "All members of the armed forces are subject to such measures," and there's also a reference to a decision of the Ministry of Defence dated the 18th of June, 1991. So quite obviously they're referring to the Ministry of Defence of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Our Defence team has tried to determine the date, to determine the source of the document. We haven't had success. Since the expert refers to it, we should know the date, the source, and who signed the document. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. That's exactly what I was thinking myself. There's no signature here. As for the dates, we have temporary instructions here. I saw that on the stamp in the B/C/S version on the top right corner there is the archive stamps, on the upper right corner of the document. Could you please tell us where this document comes from, where it was found? Was this document disclosed to you by the authorities?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think everyone in the courtroom, between you and counsel, have indicated essentially the knowledge, the information that we have about the document. It does in fact come from the Croatian State Archive. It was produced to that extent by the Republic of Croatia. It does have a reference to a document dated in 1991. That doesn't mean this document's in 1991. It does talk about the establishment of various groups that we're familiar -- I think we're familiar with at this point, the operation zone, the brigade commanders, which seem certainly consistent with what we see in the HVO and it's generated by what's simply described here as the HZ HB commander and says: "This instruction comes into effect immediately and will be applied temporarily. Alongside this instruction earlier regulations which are not contrary to the constitution and other HZ HB regulations may be applied." And that, Your Honour, that's the only other information I can provide to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Be that as it may --

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. Your Honours, then the conclusion or the answer to my question as to whether the Prosecution knows the date of the rules, well, we don't know the date of the rules. So it's very difficult to ask anything about these rules since we don't know when they existed and up until what time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. We get the point. Mr. Scott, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: General, there's really -- using the document primarily just to have you address a couple of general points for us which frankly, I think, could be addressed independent of the document, but at the end of the second paragraph, I do want to ask you about this. It says: "When issuing orders, military officers are required to take into consideration the level of training of their subordinated for the execution task stemming from the orders." Can you explain to the Judges why that would be the case and what that would mean in practical terms?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: Well, I regard that as a very common-sense statement saying that when orders are given the commander giving those orders must be cognisant of the abilities of those who he is giving the orders to. Are those orders within their competence? Have they conducted the right training? Is he happy that they could carry them out? Now, that's particularly relevant in this sort of situation with hastily raised forces of varying degrees of competence and training commanded by officers of varying degrees of background themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you give us -- I don't know if you have -- yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment, Mr. Scott. What you're saying is extremely interesting, but I have the following question about this: We may understand this in the -- in the British Army. The commander has to check that the officer he's going to give the order to will be in a position to execute these orders, to comply with these orders. But in Bosnia and Herzegovina, the situation was quite different. It was a war situation. Civilians had been mobilised, and by definition, these civilians have not received the same military training as members of the British forces, and overnight these people receive a rifle, a uniform, and -- but without having received any kind of training. Therefore, we are talking about very particular circumstances. In those circumstances, should this type of document apply?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, my view on that is that under those circumstances, the onus on the commander is even greater, because he will be aware of the limitations of the forces and, therefore, he must be extremely cognisant of what he's asking them to do, or the supervision or extra help he gives them to do it as a result.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. I don't think they're getting translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The accused don't have any translation. I believe that the question was translated but not the answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: General, let me just go back if I might and then hopefully go forward. You said a few moments ago, I believe you said: "Your Honour, my view on that is that under those circumstances, the onus on the commander is even greater, because he will be aware of the limitations of the forces and therefore he must be extremely cognisant of what he's asking them to do or the supervision or extra help he gives them to do it as a result." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: That's what I said, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And in fact, if you go to paragraph 31 of your report, I believe you essentially address just the point that was just made. You say there: "The more ad hoc the forces raised, the more difficult all this becomes, because effective performance is the product only of considerable training and preparation. In this respect, the HVO would have had a problem since there was a shortage of time to conduct proper and thorough training. This would have been apparent from the start and therefore would or should have been foremost in the minds of those responsible for delivering a properly trained force." Now, in light of what's just been said, can you comment further on that?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: Well, at the risk of repetition, I think that that says it all. Under these circumstances, I understand all too readily the problems that the HVO would have had, but therefore the responsibilities of the commanders to bear -- to bear the shortcomings and limitations of their forces in mind in the conduct of operations is even greater. To give an example, it might be all right to launch an inexperienced militia with armament against a opposing trenchline, but if you want to be certain that when the trenchline is captured all the prisoners aren't slaughtered because that's what the inexperienced and uneducated soldiers think is right, then you better be alert to that and take the appropriate actions in terms of command and control and prior briefing, et cetera, to ensure that doesn't happen. I mean, that's just an example.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Just a following up on that. So to make that a bit more concrete, what then would be -- in that situation what would be the duty and responsibility of the commanding officer when he knows he has poorly trained and perhaps poorly disciplined troops under his command?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: Well, I think, first and foremost, realising and acknowledging the shortcomings of his troops he should draw on his own experience and ask himself, Well, what are the most likely things that are going to go wrong? And ensure that properly briefing or orders which doesn't necessarily entail too much time and effort are given. So for example, these untrained forces could be well-told in the preparation for an operation that the following things are against the laws of armed conflict and are absolutely forbidden and severe disciplinary action will be taken against anybody that indulges in such practices. Such practices include, A, shooting prisoners once they have surrendered; two, raping women; three, setting fire to all the houses; four, treating civilian community in an inhumane way. That doesn't take very much time and effort, and it's the sort of briefing that could be given prior to an operation. And also in the training for any operation, those key essential points could be stressed and exercised.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Now, so far when I've asked you this question about being -- the commander being mindful of the limitations of the soldiers or troops under his command, and we've talked about that in the context of perhaps being poorly trained, but let me extend the -- my question to what is the responsibility of command -- of the commander when he has troops under his command which he knows from prior reports or information have a tendency to engage in misconduct?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: Well, if he has troops under his command who he knows have a prior tendency to indulge in misconduct, first of all he has, as required by his own doctrine, the responsibility to take action against them in advance of them doing it next time; and secondly, if there's not enough evidence but he has suspicions that they may behave in an irregular manner, to ensure that he takes whatever steps are necessary to prevent that, which may -- which may mean either not using them at all or putting them under a very powerful commander who can impress his personality on them and ensure that it doesn't happen, or put military police in with them to observe what's happening, or any one of a whole range of issues he could take action on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: General Pringle, I think we're being asked to slow down. Judge Prandler is indicating that we need to slow down a little bit, I guess for the sake of interpretation. We're getting a bit ahead of ourselves, but since this topic has come up, let me again stay with it a step longer. Can you tell the Judges what's the effect on command and control or on the discipline of an army, if, for example, the commander continues to use troops that are known to engage in this conduct but continues to use them over and over again? What message does that send?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: Well, this impinges on what in my report I've described as the command climate which is really -- stems from every act and action of the commander. If a commander uses irregular forces that are known to carry out atrocities and continues to use them when it's widely known that they carry out atrocities and he continues to use them without taking any -- any of the required legal actions to prevent that, then the command climate he is creating is one where that sort of action is fair game and that sort of action is condoned by the commander and that sort of action is the way we're going to be reacting from now on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Just before moving on, we're still tying a number of different things together here, but toward the end of paragraph 32, just to come back again to what you see in various documentation, both the JNA documents and the HVO documentation that you reviewed for the purposes of your report, you say at the end of paragraph 32: "In reading SFRY military doctrine, I've been struck by its thoroughness and its general similarity with, for example, British and NATO doctrine."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry for interrupting Mr. Scott because you're referring to a new paragraph. I have a question myself about the measures, including the first measures. I'm going to read it out in English. [In English] Members of armed forces are required to carry out the orders of superior officers pertaining to the service except for those orders whose execution would constitute a criminal act." [Interpretation] Because here you referred to illegal orders -- or, rather, you refer to irregular soldiers or individuals who tend to commit crimes, and you talked about the responsibility of the superior officers, but I'd like to ask the reverse question to the expert witness. Witness, of course I don't want to dwell too much on the legal assessment of an order, whether an order is illegal or legal. It's a very complex issue, a very theoretical issue if you talk about blind or intelligent bayonets, but my question is a practical one. You have very long experience as a commander officer. You've commanded platoons and up to divisions. You've commanded battalions and brigades, and you've been sent on tour to various regions in the world. Considering this, can you tell me if you are aware of practical cases -- of cases where soldiers, subordinates refused to obey the orders of their superior officers because these orders were illegal? And I'm thinking in particular of a situation where -- in the field, because I know that if you look at the judicial -- military judicial system, if a soldier refuses to obey an order, sometimes he does this and he might be sentenced to death. So do you have any examples that have kind?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't have any personal experience serving in the British Army of any officer or soldier, to the best of my knowledge, that has refused to obey an order on the basis that it was illegal, but I'm absolutely confident that if, for example, British soldiers, having captured an enemy position, were told to take the prisoners round the back and shoot the lot, they would refuse.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Just returning to the question that I was putting to you a few moments ago. At the end of paragraph 32 you say: "In reading SFRY military doctrine I have been struck by its thoroughness and its general similarity with, for example, British and NATO doctrine. JNA doctrine on command and control, on the roles and duties of commanders, on proper conduct and on adherence to international laws would be readily recognisable in any NATO army, and would be familiar to HVO (and HV) former officers of the JNA." And is there any further comment you can make about that?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I do apologise. I have an objection with respect to the beginning of Mr. Scott's question. He said that paragraph 32 relates to the documentation of the HVO as well. Line 23, page 56. Which is not correct. What it relates to is the documents of the JNA, and it is assumed that former JNA officers who transferred to the HVO or HV knew the doctrine.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I accept that, but I was modifying -- I was expanding the question on my feet to include references to the evidence that the witness gave earlier this afternoon that he found in the HVO documents that were very similar, expressing the same doctrine and same principles as the JNA doctrine. But be that as it may.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you comment further on the quality of the JNA doctrinal or guidance material that you saw?

utterances.speaker: ANDREW PRINGLE
utterances.text: Yes. As I've said in my report, I was struck by what I think is the excellence of the JNA doctrinal material. It's very comprehensive. It's very thorough, and it's ready recognisable to anything that I have been taught or experienced in my own military career.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, moving forward again to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Petkovic. THE ACCUSED PETKOVIC: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have an objection. JNA doctrine is being discussed and so on and so forth. Now, could we look at the doctrinary documents of the JNA which the witness has studied? So could the witness tell us which documents he studied relating to doctrine from the JNA?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I say this is cross-examination material, absolutely appropriate for cross-examination. That's fine if counsel wants to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. General Petkovic, this question may be asked as part of the cross-examination to challenge the credibility of the witness. That's part and parcel of the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, with respect, we -- we support, of course we do generally support but specifically we strongly support what our client has said on this. It is part of examination-in-chief and fair examination-in-chief to make it clear to the Defence what is being said, what sources are being used, and what is the basis of the evidence that's being given. If it's left to the Defence then to flush out this material, in effect what's happening, apart from anything else, cross -- examination-in-chief time is in effect being transferred to the Defence because we're being made to do the Prosecution's work for them. But General Petkovic's request is an entirely fair and reasonable one, Your Honour. It should be made clear as we go along if the witness is being asked to refer to material exactly what material it is he's drawing his views and conclusions from and what material they tie together with. It is a fair request, Your Honour, and with respect Your Honour should endorse and support it and require the Prosecution to do just that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, you're aware of the problem. I might ask the question myself, but you can do it too. What the Defence is saying is -- or asking is on what basis the witness can say that the JNA doctrine is similar to a NATO doctrine in these matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, I'm sorry, Your Honour, I'm operating on the assumption that everyone has read the report and I don't have to cover everything that's in the report since I tendered that at the very beginning. And if Mr. Stewart hadn't had a chance to read the report yet, maybe he can do that over --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm not going to get as thin-skinned as Mr. Scott about it; of course I've read the report. That isn't the point. The point is whether the accused themselves as we go along and all the counsel should be able fairly to follow it. Of course we've all read the report. General Petkovic has read the report many times. Of course he has, and we all have but we are entitled to know to what particular documents the witness's statements and conclusions are tied, not on every detail we're not asking that but in -- in broad terms and on important documents, on these important views and conclusions expressed by the witness, again General Petkovic's request is fair.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now about Exhibit P 00005, Exhibit P 00007, Exhibit P 08128, how about all the documents, the exhibits are cited in the report? How about that?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, with your permission I'd just like to say one sentence which sums it up. What can be considered JNA doctrine is the right of the JNA to defend the socialist federal set-up of Yugoslavia, to defend Yugoslavian territory and its territorial community, to further the policies of the League of Communists of Yugoslavia and so on and so forth. So that is the crux of JNA doctrine. And if we use the concept of JNA doctrine as something that held true for the armies engendered on the territory of the former Yugoslavia, then our clients have the right to ask these questions. What doctrines or parts of the doctrine are we dealing with? We're not challenging certain portions related to command and control that existed in the sense of guidelines, textbooks, rules and regulations governing the Yugoslavia but when we're talking about the doctrine then this must be differentiated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand that is very complex issue. Yes, I understand, Mr. Stewart. I'll put the question myself and your concerns will be addressed. Yes, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, on a slightly different point, I apologise. We both wanted to speak at once and say slightly different things. Of course, I support Ms. Alaburic but returning to what Mr. Scott said when he started listing how about exhibit number, exhibit number exhibit number, and all the documents exhibited -- that are exhibited in the report. That's precisely our point: If you don't differentiate, if you don't actually link particular documents to particular answers and particular conclusions as you go along, it's not a fair examination-in-chief because just to say see the report and see all the exhibits, that's absolutely hopeless. He's given the game away, that's in effect what they're doing. They're just dumping this stuff on -- the accused have got to deal with it as well. They're highly intelligent men, but they're not trained lawyers, Mr. Petkovic is a military man and we've all got to be able to follow from our different perspectives what's going on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I get the point. General, Ms. Alaburic said that the three documents given by the Prosecution on number 5, number 7, and 8128 are according to the Defence documents that are related to the doctrine of the former Yugoslavia, but the Defence added that at the time military doctrine had one objective, which was to defend the political system of the time and you're familiar with that system just as I am. According to the Defence, this particular political system is reflected in these documents, but the question that they put to you is on what basis based on the doctrine you derived from these three documents on what basis can you say that this also applies to the HVO and to draw a comparison with the NATO doctrine? Do you understand the logic applied here? You are saying that the HVO doctrine is almost the same as the NATO doctrine, and you use these three documents as well but what the Defence is saying is that these three documents reflect a completely different doctrine, a doctrine related to a time when the Cold War was raging and all this. We could spend hours on this; it's really interesting, but it's not really the point here. Therefore, on what basis can you move from the JNA or HVO documents to the NATO doctrine? Did you get the sense of what the Defence of General Petkovic is saying here?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, in my report I have made a statement to the effect that it is a -- my working premise that the JNA doctrine formed the basis of the doctrine that was used by all the constituent parts of the former Republic of Yugoslavia in their break-up and in the course of the war for a number of reasons, including the fact that all the members of the ethnicity armies who had been former JNA officers would have been trained and educated to that doctrine. I went on to say that in reading the doctrinal articles that I had been supplied with, all of which are referenced in detail as footnotes to my report, that I had not seen anything there with which I was not familiar or in fundamental disagreement, and I went on to say that my overall impression is that doctrine originated by the JNA and I assumed taken on by the likes of the HV, HVO, VRS, and et cetera, because their ex-regular officers would have been trained to that would be readily recognisable in a NATO context. That's not to say it's exactly the same, but there was nothing that struck me as being fundamentally contrary to anything that any French, German, Italian, Spanish, British, et cetera, officer would recognise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My colleague is going to take the floor but before let me just say if you're saying this doctrine -- well, the vectors of this doctrine with the HVO were the former officers of the JNA that had been trained in former Yugoslavia and who then went on to be either part of HVO or VH or whatever, and because of their training what they would do is apply what they had learnt in the former system. So perhaps I can quote an example that will support this. It's a bit like the British Army that trained officers in India, and when India became independent, well, the military doctrine of the former British Empire was perpetuated in India. Would -- is that how we should construe your reply, i.e., that the doctrine goes on because of the training of former officers that have gone from one army to another?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, in part, but I think also we should bear in mind that HZ HB, for example, was coming into being at the very same time as they were beginning to conduct a war, and under those circumstances you don't have the luxury of sitting back and churning out your own doctrinal manuals, and therefore you are most likely to grasp what is in existence already and what you have been trained to. Now, over time you may adapt that doctrine to be your own particular HZ HB doctrine. Over time, and when you have the time, and probably when the war is over. That's -- that's what I'm saying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge Prandler will be asking the question now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: I would like to say the following.
